video_title: Market Starting To Crack Under High Bond Yields? | Michael Lebowitz
gist: RIA Advisors' Michael Lebowitz tells Adam Taggart that a handful of AI mega-caps are masking real cracks under the surface of the market (RSP, financials, real estate and utilities already down 4-9%) as high bond yields work through the economy with a lag, while he flags Oracle's credit as an AI-bubble stress point, a Fed dot-plot that raised rate expectations without changing its economic forecasts, and a shift from 'TINA' to 'TIGA' that has RIA trimming mega-cap tech for value, utilities and 5-year bonds.

themes.theme: Rate Transmission Lag Into the Economy

insights.claim: Short-term rates hit the economy almost immediately (credit cards, floating-rate corporate debt) while long-term rates like mortgages take much longer to bite, so the Fed has been raising short rates specifically to slow the economy since it cannot directly influence oil-driven inflation.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Investors should expect the drag from this year's yield rise to keep showing up with a lag over the next year or two rather than all at once.
insights.quote: It's the cost of money. It's the cost of money that is that is everything.

insights.claim: A large wave of corporate bonds issued in 2021 near 2-2.5% coupons is maturing through 2025-2027 and refinancing at rates near 6% or higher, forcing companies to cut capex, close stores and lay off workers to protect margins.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Watch corporate maturity walls and margin guidance for signs that debt refinancing costs are starting to force operating cuts.

insights.claim: Lebowitz frames the current tightening cycle under the maxim 'higher rates beget lower rates': the very act of pushing yields up slows the economy enough, both in the US and globally, that it eventually forces yields back down.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A framework for timing eventual rate-cut and bond-rally trades: the higher and faster yields rise now, the sooner and larger the reversal is likely to be.

themes.theme: Market Internals Are Weaker Than the Index Shows

insights.claim: While the S&P 500 looks calm near all-time highs, the equal-weighted S&P (RSP) is down about 4%, with financials down 5%, small caps down 6.5%, real estate down 7%, and utilities down 9%, showing that rate-sensitive sectors are already feeling the pain the headline index hides.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Don't read index-level calm as broad market health; check equal-weight and sector breadth before assuming risk is contained.
insights.quote: RSP is down 4% financials 5% short um small caps 6 and a half% real estate seven utilities nine

insights.claim: RIA's sector rotation model shows technology (XLK) alone in the overbought/outperforming quadrant while XLU, XLY, real estate, transportation, financials, staples, industrials and materials cluster in the weak, underperforming quadrant, and the dispersion between sectors is at an extreme that has historically preceded S&P pullbacks.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A sector-dispersion extreme like this has previously marked local market tops; it's a signal worth tracking rather than dismissing as noise.

insights.claim: Lebowitz's 'LeBron James and four skeletons' analogy: a handful of AI mega-caps are carrying the S&P like a superstar still scoring 50-60 points a game, but if rising rates finally 'injure' the leaders, the rest of the roster has shown it can't pick up the scoring slack.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Index-level risk is concentrated in a small number of mega-cap leaders; their earnings and rate sensitivity now matter disproportionately to the whole market.
insights.quote: LeBron's being triple teamed and all those other guys are out there but they're not scoring because LeBron's still scoring 50 60 points a game

insights.claim: RIA already began rotating its own portfolio this week, trimming its large-cap/mega-cap tech position and adding to value and utilities, in anticipation that leadership rotates away from tech as rates stay elevated.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A live example of a systematic factor-rotation trade being executed in response to the tech/everything-else divergence, worth watching for follow-through.

insights.claim: Today's AI data-center buildout is compared to the dot-com era's fiber-optic buildout: companies like Global Crossing and MCI laid the physical groundwork for the modern internet but went bankrupt because revenue arrived too slowly relative to their spending and debt.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: The infrastructure being built now could still prove valuable long-term even if the specific companies funding it today don't survive to profit from it, exactly as happened with fiber.

insights.claim: Google, Meta and Microsoft differ from the dot-com telecom bankruptcies because they have largely funded data-center capex out of existing profits rather than debt, though they are increasingly starting to borrow or raise equity to fund further buildout.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Watch hyperscaler debt issuance and equity raises as a leading indicator of whether the AI capex cycle is starting to outrun free cash flow.

insights.claim: Oracle is flagged as the clearest credit risk in the AI buildout: its bonds are trading at junk-like yields near 9-10% (or higher), and CDS markets are pricing in a real chance of default, making it a race between incoming AI revenue and its debt maturity timeline.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Oracle's credit spreads and CDS pricing are a concrete, trackable proxy for market sentiment on AI-buildout revenue timing risk, distinct from the safer hyperscalers.

insights.claim: The biggest risk to markets over the next year or two is not an outright AI bust but hyperscalers voluntarily throttling capex plans (e.g. building five data centers instead of seven) if revenue doesn't show up fast enough.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A capex slowdown announcement from a major hyperscaler, rather than a hard AI collapse, is the more probable near-term catalyst for a market correction.
insights.quote: Let's hold off. Let's just build five data centers instead of seven, right?

insights.claim: Because AI-related spending now represents a large share of both index market cap and GDP growth, a 20-30% slowdown in AI capex could be large enough to trigger a 20-25% stock market correction.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Investors should size position risk around AI capex growth rates, not just AI earnings, since capex deceleration alone could be the correction trigger.

insights.claim: Historical efficiency gains akin to Moore's Law could shrink data centers dramatically over time (from the size of a football field toward an office or even a phone), which lowers future capex intensity but also risks leaving today's newly built data centers prematurely outdated.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Today's AI infrastructure spend carries obsolescence risk analogous to hardware depreciation, separate from the revenue-timing risk already being debated.

insights.claim: Cheaper open-source and free AI models (including options coming out of China, plus free Gemini) are already pulling routine usage away from frontier paid models, and lower per-query token costs mean total compute demand and revenue for heavy-spending AI labs could grow more slowly than expected.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Model commoditization is a real earnings risk specifically for the AI labs carrying the most spending and debt (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI), separate from hyperscaler infrastructure risk.
insights.quote: If those models are become somewhat commoditized and interchangeable, especially with much cheaper models, that becomes a big problem given their debt loads.

themes.theme: Fed Policy and Bond Market Signals

insights.claim: At its most recent meeting the Fed raised its median projection for where Fed funds will settle next year by roughly half a percentage point (from about 3.6% to 4.1%) without changing its inflation or unemployment forecasts, an internally inconsistent signal since the whole rationale for the hike is to slow inflation and the economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A dot-plot that raises the rate path without changing the economic outlook suggests the Fed itself is uncertain or signaling for reasons beyond its stated inflation mandate; treat forward guidance with skepticism.
insights.quote: if you're telling me that higher rates have no impact on the economy, why are you changing rates?

insights.claim: Fed funds futures show no market consensus on the rate path a year out, pricing in roughly 75-100 basis points of further hikes over the next several months alongside real uncertainty about whether cuts could follow quickly if the Fed is seen as having made a policy mistake.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Wide dispersion in futures pricing itself is a source of bond-market volatility; watch CME Fed funds futures for shifts in that consensus.

insights.claim: The real (inflation-adjusted) yield is a better restrictiveness gauge than the nominal yield: a 5-year Treasury near 5% minus a roughly 2.3% breakeven inflation rate leaves a real yield near 2.7%, which is historically quite restrictive across mortgages, auto loans and corporate borrowing.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Judge monetary restrictiveness off real yields (nominal minus TIPS breakeven), not off whether nominal yields look 'high' or 'low' in isolation.
insights.quote: compare it to break even inflation rates to get a much better feel for how restrictive it is.

insights.claim: Over the past month the 2-year yield rose almost 50 basis points while the 30-year rose only about 6 basis points and the 10-year about 25 basis points, meaning the yield surge is concentrated in the short-to-intermediate 'belly' of the curve, which is exactly where Fed-fund-sensitive mortgages and corporate loans get repriced.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: The economic pain from this yield move is concentrated where floating and intermediate-term borrowing resets, not primarily in long-duration assets.

insights.claim: Core CPI (about 2.4%) and core PCE (about 3.4%) are viewed as the more reliable inflation gauges right now because headline inflation is being distorted by oil and diesel prices tied to the Iran conflict rather than by domestic demand the Fed can actually influence.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Don't expect Fed policy to address oil-driven headline inflation; the Fed can only address it by crushing demand, so oil-driven spikes are a separate risk to track from core trend inflation.

themes.theme: From TINA to TIGA: Credit Over Equities

insights.claim: Lebowitz describes markets moving from 'TINA' (there is no alternative to equities, when bond yields were near zero) to 'TIGA' (there is a good alternative), meaning investors can now lock in roughly 5% bond yields instead of relying solely on richly-valued equities to meet financial goals.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Reallocating a larger share of a goals-based portfolio into bonds yielding around 5% can meet return targets with materially less risk than staying fully exposed to expensive equities.
insights.quote: we're going from TINA to TIGA. Tina is there is no alternative.

insights.claim: RIA's trade this week was selling part of its longer-duration bond position to buy newly-auctioned 5-year Treasuries near 5%, valuing the built-in optionality that short/intermediate bonds can be sold to buy cheap stocks if equities fall 20-40% while still returning close to 5% a year even in the worst case.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A 5-year Treasury position at current yields offers a rare combination of locked-in income and real optionality to buy equities cheaply in a selloff.

insights.claim: Given today's high equity valuations, Lebowitz sees 10-year forward equity returns as likely 'negligible' regardless of the path taken to get there, whether markets rally another 30% before a steep drawdown or fall sharply now before a strong multi-year recovery.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Investors relying on average historical equity returns over the next decade should stress-test that assumption given current starting valuations.
insights.quote: we could be up 30% for the next three years before we fall 80% for two years and then just go on a nice steady 5% rise. Or we could fall 90% the rest of this year and then have a great nine years ahead of us.

themes.theme: A Frozen, K-Shaped Labor Market and Economy

insights.claim: The labor market is effectively frozen: JOLTS hiring rates are low and declining and payroll growth is very slow, even though headline unemployment stays near full employment, meaning few people are being laid off but few are finding new jobs either, leaving little cushion if layoffs do accelerate.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Low headline unemployment is masking underlying labor market fragility; a hiring freeze with no cushion means any layoff wave could push unemployment up faster than usual.

insights.claim: The US economy looks 'K-shaped': AI data-center capex is estimated to be adding roughly 4 percentage points to headline GDP growth this year, while growth excluding that spending has been close to flat.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Headline GDP strength is heavily dependent on continued AI capex; any slowdown in that spending would expose how weak the rest of the economy actually is.
insights.quote: Strip out the data center growth and we've had almost no economic growth.

themes.theme: Oil and Geopolitics as the Market's Wildcard

insights.claim: Elevated oil and diesel prices tied to the ongoing conflict involving Iran are viewed as the single biggest swing factor for both bond yields and the stock market right now, more so than the Fed's own policy moves.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Track crude oil and diesel prices as a leading indicator for bond yields and equity risk sentiment, potentially more informative near-term than Fed statements.

insights.claim: Lebowitz expects the House to flip Democratic in the midterms with the Senate becoming a toss-up, and views the resulting legislative gridlock as double-edged: it prevents further deficit spending but also blocks needed legislation, making it a secondary market driver behind oil prices.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Political gridlock risk is being deprioritized relative to oil-driven interest rate risk as a market driver heading into the midterms.

insights.claim: Lebowitz generally agrees that geopolitical events don't usually drive market direction, but argues this particular conflict is different because of its direct, sustained pass-through into crude oil prices, which then spreads into interest rates and equities.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Unlike most geopolitical shocks, this one has a durable transmission mechanism into markets via oil, so a resolution (or escalation) could move yields and equities materially.
